questions.title: What exactly is the purpose of the normalizer state $n_t$ in sLSTM and how does it affect the hidden state computation?
questions.question_body: In the sLSTM forward equations (Eq. 3) we see that the hidden state is computed as $	ilde{h}_t = c_t / n_t$, where $n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t$. I understand that this normalizer is introduced to stabilize exponential gates, but I’m not clear on how it influences the dynamics of $c_t$. Does $n_t$ act as a running sum of future forget gates, effectively divided by the accumulated input gate values? Why is this necessary when exponential gating could already yield large values?

questions.title: How does exponential gating improve a LSTM's ability to revise storage decisions?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that switching from sigmoid to exponential activations on the input and forget gates enables revision of stored information (e.g., the Nearest Neighbor Search task). Could someone explain, in plain terms, why exponential gates allow a later input to overwrite an earlier stored value? How does this differ from the standard LSTM behavior where gates are bounded by zero and one?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind introducing a matrix memory in mLSTM versus a scalar memory in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: mLSTM stores a key-value pair using a covariance update $C_t = C_{t-1} + v_t k_t^	op$, while sLSTM keeps a scalar cell. Why does turning the memory into a $d 	imes d$ matrix increase storage capacity? Is it analogous to having multiple independent scalar cells, or does it provide richer interactions between keys and values? Also, how does this relate to Fast Weight Programmers?

questions.title: Why is the mLSTM forward pass fully parallelizable while sLSTM is not?
questions.question_body: The paper states that mLSTM has no memory mixing and hence can be reformulated in parallel. In contrast, sLSTM contains hidden‑to‑hidden recurrent connections that break parallelism. Could someone walk through how the recurrence in Eq. (10) prevents vector‑wise parallel execution, whereas Eq. (8) allows it? How do the CUDA kernels take advantage of this difference?

questions.title: "Exponential gating" vs. "squashing": why use $	ilde{h}_t = c_t / n_t$ instead of $	anh(c_t)$ in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: Standard LSTMs use an activation $	ilde{h}_t = 	anh(c_t)$ to keep $c_t$ bounded. In sLSTM we replace this with a division by $n_t$. What practical difference does this make for gradient flow or numerical stability? Are there any situations where $	anh(c_t)$ would be preferable?

questions.title: Does using a covariance update rule in mLSTM cause information loss compared to exact key‑value storage?
questions.question_body: The covariance update $	riangle C = v k^	op$ seems similar to Hebbian learning. If we only ever perform outer products and later evaluate $C q$, could we end up with interference among stored pairs? How does this compare to an explicit attention mechanism which computes softmax weights over all key vectors?

questions.title: How are residual block architectures chosen for xLSTM blocks (post vs pre up‑projection), and what effect does this have on performance?
questions.question_body: "sLSTM" uses post‑up‑projection blocks while "mLSTM" uses pre‑up‑projection blocks according to Section 3.4.2. What guides this design choice? Does placing up‑projection before or after recurrent processing affect numerical stability or expressivity?

questions.title: "xLSTM[7:1]" vs "xLSTM[1:0]": how does changing the ratio of mLSTM to sLSTM blocks trade off capacity and speed?
questions.question_body: "xLSTM[7:1]" means 7 mLSTM blocks out of 8 total; "xLSTM[1:0]" uses only one xLSTM block presumably sLSTM or something else? The notation is confusing – what exactly do these acronyms mean, and how does varying this ratio impact model perplexity, parallelism, and compute cost?

questions.title: "Stabilization state" $m_t$ – when exactly should I use $	ilde{i}_t - m_t$ instead of $	ilde{i}_t$ for exponential gates?
questions.question_body: Equation (5) shows a stabilizer state and adjusted gates $i'_t$, $f'_t$. The paper claims replacing $f_t$ with $f'_t$ and $i_t$ with $i'_t$ does not change outputs or gradients. Under what circumstances is this adjustment necessary? For example, should I always compute with stabilized gates when training large models with exponential activations?

questions.title: "Memory mixing" – how does it differ from the traditional cell-to-cell mixing seen in multi‑cell LSTMs?
questions.question_body: "sLSTM can have multiple memory cells…memory mixing via recurrent connections R_z, R_i…with exponential gating as an effect." How exactly are these matrices applied; do they mix cell states directly or only through gated inputs? Is there any overlap with Gated Linear Units or other gated RNN designs?

questions.title: "Maximum over future forget gates" – clarification on correct implementation
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that the normalizer state sums 'the product of the input gate times all future forget gates'. However Eq. (3) updates $n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t$. Is this equivalent to accumulating product terms over future time steps? If so, could you give an algebraic derivation showing that expansion yields $ rac{c_T}{n_T}$ equals some weighted average over past inputs adjusted by forget products?
